reports.content: In this article From exposed secrets to cloud compromise Follow-on actions Mitigating application credential abuse activity Defending against agentic AI attacks Microsoft detections Advanced hunting queries Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization. Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. reports.content: Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth. I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions. First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. Second, the focus is more local and European. Major topics were (of course) AI for defense tooling, securing AI systems themselves, and post-quantum cryptography. And here comes the local touch (in my opinion): digital sovereignty and regulatory compliance, with NIS2, CRA, and DORA. But local doesn't translate to small, or to the city of Nuremberg. With more than 1,000 exhibitors and 33,000 visitors from 70 countries over three days of exhibition, preceded by a congress day, it was huge. Even as a trade show veteran, I was overwhelmed. My conversations at the booth had a different focus, though. It was a lot of chatter about vulnerabilities like php2shell or broccoli2shell and state-sponsored actors, but again with a local touch: education. I was very surprised how many teenagers stopped by to ask for advice. Here in Germany, you mainly have two paths for your career. One is the university route, and the other is vocational (apprenticeship). Across all industries the split is roughly 50 / 50 , while in IT it is more like 80% university, 20% apprenticeship. The common minimum age to start university is 18, while it is 16 for apprenticeships. Reality is way more complex, but the details don’t matter for the point I want to make. For university opportunities in cyber, I count close to 30 bachelor programs . For apprenticeships, I count ZERO. There is the "IT Specialist" (Fachinformatiker), but it only has specializations like application development, system integration, digital networking, or data and process analysis. That is why an initiative exists to get an "IT Security" specialization going. Even the degree route is thin. There are no official statistics, but my guess is 800 to 900 graduates a year, compared to a demand of more than 100,000. reports.content: On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration , and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now , which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security. Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now. Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation. Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure. This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default. Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain. Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. reports.content: Endpoint administrators need to keep elevated access accountable at scale. Security teams also need a clearer view of expert-led protection and a simpler way to deploy SQL Server protection in Azure Government. As AI agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to limit their authority and adapt protection as risk changes. This month’s Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender updates introduce capabilities across these areas, alongside new Secure AI capabilities for agent access. A recent Secure Now update in Microsoft Security Exposure Management also connects information on recent threats to focused initiatives for reducing exposure. Here’s what’s new: Limit agent authority to the task with Dynamic Permissions Give agents task-scoped authority and adapt access as risk changes As agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to manage what each agent is allowed to do. Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires. As the agent works, Dynamic Agent Risk assesses whether the agent’s authority aligns with changing behavior and context. Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond proportionately by narrowing permissions, restricting access to resources, or requiring human approval for higher-impact actions. Together, these capabilities are designed to help organizations tailor agent authority before an agent acts and adjust access as risk changes. See how security can respond when an agent steps outside its task. Contain local AI agents with Microsoft Execution Containers Apply least-privilege boundaries to help limit access on Windows Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, gives organizations an operating system-enforced containment layer for AI agents, designed to limit what an agent can access. Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions, with additional isolation options for higher-risk scenarios. Organizations can tune and validate policies before enforcing them broadly, while upcoming integration with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Agent 365 is intended to extend governance and attribution across the enterprise. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments. Q2 in review Shifting tactics and other trends › Figure 1. Monthly detected email threat volume (January – September 2026) The quarter also highlighted how sender identity and security exceptions can shape the outcome of detected threats. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. In Microsoft Teams, attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities while continuing to use live interactions for social engineering. Across malicious attachment activity more broadly, credential theft remained the dominant objective in Q3. Two campaigns observed during the quarter illustrate the range of activity behind these trends. reports.content: USN-8955-1 fixed vulnerabilities in nginx in Ubuntu 26.10, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. This update provides the corresponding update for Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Ubuntu 18.04 LTS, Ubuntu 16.04 LTS, and Ubuntu 14.04 LTS. In addition, this update fixes CVE-2026-42533 for these releases. reports.summary: Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation? Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders alr
reports.content: Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter. The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments , examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery. Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation? Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path. The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.” At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively. What should security leaders measure instead? Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively. reports.title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
reports.summary: Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an A
reports.content: Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider. What is ISO/IEC 42001? ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle. This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active. Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important? AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products? ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability. It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point. As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model . reports.content: Introduction to BOD 26-04 On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers. This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all. What did CISA actually change? BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context. Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't. The four variables to BOD 26-04 BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA): Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network? KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog? Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation? Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)? reports.content: In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. reports.content: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscape Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Impact, exposure and where to focus Next in line How Microsoft Security helps defenders act References Learn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification

This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-own
reports.content: VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage. After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token. reports.content: Overview An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required. The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain , and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc . An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider. We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets. We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046 , revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3 . The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0 , is separate from the Remote Support application version. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser , UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user. reports.content: Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.” NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session. In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies. NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows. Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline. NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2. reports.title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
reports.summary: Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond.
reports.content: October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months. A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report , the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed. At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish. For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. reports.content: Overview On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497 , an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x , 24.x , and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2 . An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder. On October 27, 2026, CVE-2026-111497 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. Given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation. Technical overview CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write ( CWE-787 ) and an unchecked return value ( CWE-252 ). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory. The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10 , 1.1.0 before 1.1.1 , and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1 . The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below. Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun , Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET , Envoy and Istio , brotli4j , and operating-system packages . Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisor

reports.content: In this article Attack overview Technical details Mitigation and protection guidance Indicators of compromise References Learn More On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough. Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy. Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present. This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. reports.summary: Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Dubbed "php2shell" and triggered by a simple HTTP request, this vulnerability affects every build since 5.4. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.
reports.content: Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Head on down to ‘The One Big Thing’. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset. But if you want a bit of levity, here’s what I wrote before everything kicked off yesterday: Ever feel like the world is moving too fast to keep up? Well, I bring you scientific proof that it’s not just you. For millions of years, the moon has been slowing down the Earth’s rotation. But over the past decade, we’ve been speeding up (I KNEW I was aging faster than before). Apparently, changes in the Earth’s core are involved (either that, or the 1978 Superman film was a documentary). This is all causing massive headaches for the people responsible for keeping time. They’re officially called “The International Bureau of Weights and Measures”, but I’m going to call them “The Time-Keepers”. For nerd reasons). The issue is that the atomic clocks that power so many of our systems, and the rotation of our planet, don’t always agree. Atomic clocks keep extremely consistent time, while each Earth day is rarely the same length as the next. Atomic timekeeping absolutely cannot stand that level of flexibility (have a watch of our “The Light We Keep” documentary to see the importance that accurate clocks have on critical infrastructure). To keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is based on atomic clocks, aligned with Earth’s rotation, we introduced a “leap second” in 1972. This system allows for an extra second to be added, or taken away, when we stray too far from atomic time. A few days ago, The Time-Keepers voted to officially abolish the leap second. Why? reports.title: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
reports.summary: This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ expos
reports.content: Cisco Talos is aware of eight compromised intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra . Rather than possessing the mandatory 384 bits of pseudo-random security, several private keys evaluated single-digit and double-digit integers. This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Six of the TLS certificates, trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have been blocked by these vendors already. Two other certificates, used for codesigning by Microsoft, have also been blocked. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ exposure. Following the disclosure, eMudhra has revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Compromise details The cause of this issue, originated during an April 30, 2025 key generation activity conducted by eMudhra under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services. During a key generation ceremony for 24 subordinate CAs, a flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process created a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step. Those keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw took the encryption from 384 bytes of entropy down to 3 – 8, making recovering the private keys trivial. reports.content: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges. CVE CVSSv4 Description CVE-2026-109618 9.2 (Critical) RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619 9.2 (Critical) RCE via stale global state All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs. The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon. Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. reports.content: Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days. For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window? Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated. The exploitation window has narrowed, big time Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines , these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent. reports.content: Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model. Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited. We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines. With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains. reports.title: Your Next Insider Threat Won’t be Human: Securing AI Agents From the Outside in
reports.summary: You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own
reports.content: Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls. The new privileged user in your environment Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all. Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy. The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice. Why agents break the trust model we had With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read. Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today. The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy . This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. Users can track assets, maintenance work orders, real estate lease information, and desk or room reservations. reports.content: Overview In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments. The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material. The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline. Key findings The first confirmed root execution occurred shortly after attacker-controlled text was inserted into a NetScaler authentication username. The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot. After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root. The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases. The attacker set /bin/sh to mode 6555, allowing an unprivileged web process to obtain effective root privileges. The implant framework maintained access through cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, an outbound reverse agent, and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy. HA synchronization and forced failover logic attempted to preserve access across the appliance pair. A Go tool mapped internal routes, DNS, LDAP/AD, management services and VMware vCenter systems. NetScaler configuration, historical configurations, HTTP configuration, diagnostics and system backup material were staged for exfiltration. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. reports.title: Rapid7 Intelligence Wins the 2026 Péter Szőr Award for Outstanding Research
reports.summary: This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabi
reports.content: Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone , was of the latter kind. Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud. What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package. What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better. Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments. The research behind the award The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever. Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company. Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion.

reports.title: How Multi-Campus Universities can Build a more Connected Security Program
reports.summary: If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where
reports.content: Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape : universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act. This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere. That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence. Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution. Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system. A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another. As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time. Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster

reports.content: Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse... Let's look at some numbers: We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 ( CVE-2014-125110 ), or even hit seven digits in 2015 ( CVE-2015-1000013 ), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.) So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers: They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts. CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%. This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. reports.content: This research was conducted jointly with Julian-Ferdinand Vögele of Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Details of the joint research and presentation are available here . Cisco Talos identified UAT-6275 ( TAG-193 by Recorded Future) activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
